newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Prospects brighten for WTO accord on infotech.
newsitem.headline: Prospects brighten for WTO accord on infotech.

text.p: Brighter prospects of agreeing a lucrative accord on free trade in technologies buoyed big powers on Tuesday at a World Trade Organisation (WTO) meeting still clouded by rows on issues from cheap labour to corruption.

The United States and the European Union announced progress in resolving their differences over a pact to eliminate tariffs on a wide range of information technology, Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky told reporters.

"We have made progress," Barshefsky said before a meeting of the Big Four major trade powers -- the United States, the EU, Japan and Canada -- on the sidelines of the first WTO ministerial conference.
EU Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan also told reporters that breakfast talks between him and Barshefsky on the second day of the conference, which ends on Friday, had gone well.
Asked whether an agreement was at hand, Brittan said: "Not yet, but we are making good progress."

However, some developing nations remained opposed to the Information Technology Agreement (ITA) to remove all tariffs in trade in computers and microchips in a sector valued at $600 billion a year by the turn of the century.

"I doubt if there will be concrete agreements coming out this week," Philippine Trade and Industry Secretary Cesar Bautista told reporters when asked about prospects for an ITA by Friday. "It's too fast for us."
Host Singapore and Malaysia have said a timetable of tariff-free trade by 2000 is too ambitious a goal.
Signals from negotiators left little doubt the major traders were aiming for agreement this week -- perhaps by Wednesday.

Japan's Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda told the second day of the conference he hoped "ardently...that we will have an agreement as the most significant achievement of this ministerial conference in the area of trade liberalisation".

The 128 full delegations from WTO member countries and ministers and officials from nearly 30 others waiting to be admitted to the organisation have also heard ringing appeals for progress to a telecoms liberalisation pact.
Negotiators at WTO headquarters in Geneva face a deadline to finalise a deal among some 50 countries by mid-February.
This sector, heavily protected in many emerging economies, is estimated to be worth well over $500 billion annually.

Battles raged behind the scenes between North and South over corruption in trade, agriculture, investment rules and competition policy and Washington served notice it would push to get the explosive issue of labour rights onto the WTO agenda.

Signs of consensus on discussing competition policy emerged at a meeting of 25 delegation heads, including the United States, Japan, the EU and many Asian nations and chaired by WTO Secretary-General Renato Ruggiero, a Japanese official said.
"No one was totally opposed to taking up the issue," the official said. "We are moving towards a compromise."

Trying to disperse the storm clouds and counter lobbying by Western-based aid groups, WTO chief economist Richard Blackhurst insisted that the poorest nations stood to reap major benefit from the freeing of global commerce.
"There has been a lot of talk about the least-developed countries (LDCs) being net losers in this process. The reality is very different," Blackhurst told a news briefing.

Ministers and their aides from different areas of the globe were meeting in conclave to try to hammer out the final text of a declaration to wrap up the gathering of the two-year-old body on Friday. Sixteen of the 20 paragraphs have been agreed.

Officials said negotiating on whether the declaration, meant to point the WTO down the free trade path into the 21st century, should include any reference at all to the labour issue was being left to last.

Several key emerging economies -- including India, Malaysia and Indonesia -- insist there should be no mention, arguing that even a neutral phrasing would suggest work conditions were a subject for the WTO.
